claim: The DELETE /v1/export-schedules/{id} path is not tenant-scoped: `(*exportHandler).delete` never reads `auth.OrgFromContext` and `(*Store).Delete` runs `DELETE FROM export_schedules WHERE id = $1` with no `org_id` predicate, so an authenticated caller from one org can delete another org's schedule by its id.

`(*Store).Delete` discards the `sql.Result` from `ExecContext`, so `(*exportHandler).delete` answers 204 for an id that matched no row, making a deletion that removed nothing indistinguishable from one that removed a schedule.

`exports.Destination` tags `AccessKey`/`SecretKey` as ordinary JSON fields with no redaction or response DTO, so `create` and `list` serialize the customer's destination bucket credentials back in their responses, contradicting docs/scheduled-exports.md's statement that the credentials are never handed back by the API.

Nothing caps how many export schedules one org can create — `(*exportHandler).create` performs no per-org count check and the `export_schedules` table carries no count or uniqueness constraint — so a single authenticated org can install unbounded permanent recurring work for the worker.

`(*exportHandler).create` decodes the request body with a bare `json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&body)`: there is no `http.MaxBytesReader` bounding the body and no `DisallowUnknownFields`, so an arbitrarily large payload is buffered into memory and a misspelled key such as `time_zone` is silently dropped instead of rejected.

`HourOfDay int` in `create`'s request struct uses Go's zero value as both "field absent" and the legitimate hour 0, so a request that omits `hour_of_day` is indistinguishable from one explicitly asking for midnight, unlike `Timezone` which gets an explicit default.

`(*Schedule).Validate` never checks that `Timezone` resolves through `time.LoadLocation` or that `Destination.Region` is non-empty, and `NextRun` swallows the `LoadLocation` error into `loc = time.UTC`, so an invalid IANA zone is accepted at the API boundary and silently runs in UTC despite the documentation requiring an IANA name.
`GET /v1/export-schedules` is unpaginated: `(*Store).ListByOrg` selects every row for the org with no limit or cursor and `(*exportHandler).list` serializes all of them.

No route or store method ever changes `Schedule.Enabled` after creation, so there is no way to pause a schedule and the only way to stop one is to delete it, losing the stored destination credentials with it.

The first run of a new schedule exports rows from before the schedule existed, because `NextRunAt` is set from creation time while `Worker.export` always reaches one full `window(s.Cadence)` back from the run start — up to seven days for a weekly schedule.

The newly added HTTP handlers, `Store` and its methods (`NewStore`, `Create`, `ListByOrg`, `Due`, `query`, `Record`, `Delete`), and the `Worker` ship with no tests, since internal/exports/exports_test.go covers only `Validate`, `NextRun`, `objectKey` and `formatValue`.

docs/scheduled-exports.md says the worker "polls every 30 seconds and takes whatever is due", but Worker.tick calls store.Due with dueBatchSize = 25, so more than 25 due schedules leave the remainder for a later tick.

`Store.Due` selects due rows with a plain SELECT — no FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, no lease or claim column, no transaction spanning the read and the later `Store.Record` write, which only advances `next_run_at` after the export has finished — so every live worker selects and runs the same due schedule, contradicting docs/scheduled-exports.md, which states a schedule is claimed by one worker and a due run happens once even with several workers live.

`Destination.AccessKey` and `Destination.SecretKey` carry ordinary JSON tags (access_key / secret_key) with no suppression and `Schedule` embeds `Destination` by value, so `exportHandler.create` and `exportHandler.list`, which marshal whole `Schedule` values, return the customer's bucket credentials in every create and list response — contradicting docs/scheduled-exports.md, which states the credentials are never handed back by the API.

`Store.Create` inserts `Destination.AccessKey` and `Destination.SecretKey` verbatim into the plain TEXT columns `dest_access_key` / `dest_secret_key`, with no encryption anywhere in the change, contradicting docs/scheduled-exports.md, which states the destination credentials are stored encrypted.

`Schedule.Validate` checks name, dataset, format, cadence, hour and destination but never `Timezone`, so an unloadable zone name is accepted at the API boundary and `NextRun` silently substitutes UTC in its `if err != nil { loc = time.UTC }` branch — a fail-open that `exports_test.go`'s case named 'unknown timezone falls back to UTC' pins as intended behaviour, while docs/scheduled-exports.md tells customers the value must be an IANA name.

`Schedule.Validate` requires `Destination.Bucket` and both credentials but never checks `Destination.Region`, and the migration's `dest_region TEXT NOT NULL` admits the empty string, so an empty or arbitrary caller-supplied region is stored and only reaches `storage.NewClient` inside the worker.

`Store.Delete` runs `DELETE FROM export_schedules WHERE id = $1` with no `org_id` predicate and `exportHandler.delete` never reads the org from the request context, so any authenticated caller can delete another tenant's schedule by guessing its integer id — unlike the sibling read path `Store.ListByOrg`, which does scope on `org_id`.
`Store.Delete` and `Store.Record` discard the `sql.Result`, so a delete matching no row is indistinguishable from a real deletion and still yields 204, and a `Record` matching no row reports success.

`Store.query` builds its statement by concatenating a caller-supplied `where` SQL fragment into the query string rather than taking a fixed statement, so the signature invites a future caller to interpolate untrusted input even though today's callers pass only hardcoded literals.

`Store.Due`'s `ORDER BY next_run_at LIMIT $2` orders on a key that is not unique — schedules sharing a cadence and hour tie exactly — so which rows the batch takes from a tied group is undefined, and a tied group larger than `dueBatchSize` can return the same subset on every poll.

Nothing bounds how many schedules a single org may create and `Store.Due` takes the globally oldest `dueBatchSize` rows with no per-org fairness while `Worker.tick` processes the batch sequentially, so one org's schedules can monopolise every batch.

`internal/exports/exports_test.go` covers only `Validate`, `NextRun`, `objectKey` and `formatValue`, so `Store` and all of its database methods, the `Worker` with its export/serialize path, and the three HTTP handlers ship with no tests at all.

`Schedule.Enabled` is persisted, indexed and used as `Store.Due`'s predicate and is hardcoded to `true` by `exportHandler.create`, but no route or store method can ever set it to false, so the only way to stop a schedule is to delete it.

`Schedule.LastError` is populated verbatim from `err.Error()` in `Worker.runSchedule` and returned by `GET /v1/export-schedules`, so raw storage-client and database error text — including internal schema names, endpoints and request details — reaches the customer.

The comment above `datasets` claims anything not in the map is rejected before it ever reaches the worker, but `Worker.export` interpolates `datasets[s.Dataset]` for a schedule re-read from the database, where a missing key yields an empty table name and a malformed statement rather than a named refusal.

`Store.ListByOrg` returns every row for an org with no limit or pagination, and the migration's only index is `idx_export_schedules_due ON (next_run_at) WHERE enabled`, so `WHERE org_id = $1 ORDER BY id` has no index behind it.

`Schedule.Validate` imposes no length or content constraint on the free-text fields — `Name` is only rejected when blank and `Destination.Prefix` is not checked at all — so arbitrarily long or structured values, including path segments and control characters, are stored in unbounded TEXT columns and concatenated into the object key.

The cadence vocabulary hourly/daily/weekly is spelled out as bare string literals in `Validate`, `NextRun`, `window` and the migration's CHECK constraint rather than as a named type with constants the way `Format` is, and `window`'s `default` branch silently returns the 24-hour window for any cadence it does not recognise.

The destination credentials are stored in cleartext — `dest_access_key` and `dest_secret_key` are plain `TEXT` columns that `Store.Create` binds and `Store.query` scans unmodified, with no encryption, envelope, or KMS step anywhere in the change — while `docs/scheduled-exports.md` tells customers the destination credentials are stored encrypted.

The migration's only index is the partial `idx_export_schedules_due ON export_schedules (next_run_at) WHERE enabled`, which serves the worker's `Due` query, so `Store.ListByOrg`'s `WHERE org_id = $1 ORDER BY id` has no supporting index.

`CREATE TABLE export_schedules` gives `format` and `cadence` a `CHECK (... IN (...))` matching `Schedule.Validate` but leaves the other columns whose domains `Validate` also enforces — `dataset`, `hour_of_day`, `timezone` — unconstrained at the database level, so the domain-enforcement pattern is applied to only some of the table's peer columns.
`migrations/0057_export_schedules.sql` contains only the forward `CREATE TABLE` and `CREATE INDEX` inside `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`, with no down or rollback counterpart.
`migrations/0057_export_schedules.sql` adds no uniqueness constraint on a schedule's identity, so one org can hold two identical schedules whose runs contend for the same object key.
`last_status` and `last_error` default to `''`, an in-band sentinel that makes "has never run" indistinguishable from a run that recorded an empty value on `GET /v1/export-schedules`.

The `enabled` column that `Store.Due` filters on and the partial index is built on can never become false, because `exportHandler.create` hardcodes `Enabled: true` and the change adds no update route or store method that writes it.

The three new `/v1/export-schedules` routes registered in `NewRouter` (`internal/api/router.go`) are mounted behind `authed` inside `withRequestID(withRecovery(mux))` with no rate limiting applied to them.

Nothing in the change bounds how many export schedules one org may hold: neither `exportHandler.create`, `Schedule.Validate`, `Store.Create`, nor `migrations/0057_export_schedules.sql` imposes a per-org cap or count constraint, so each accepted row adds another recurring window scan and upload.

In `NextRun` (internal/exports/schedule.go), the daily/weekly path builds the fire time with `time.Date(..., s.HourOfDay, 0, 0, 0, loc)` and advances it with `AddDate(0, 0, 1)`, so on a DST transition day the configured local hour is silently normalised — a spring-forward hour that does not exist is moved to a neighbouring instant, and a fall-back hour that occurs twice resolves to one of them unspecified — making the run fire at an hour other than the one configured.

In `NextRun` (internal/exports/schedule.go), the hourly branch `local.Add(time.Hour).Truncate(time.Hour).UTC()` truncates against absolute time rather than the wall clock in `loc`, so the `from.In(loc)` conversion has no effect on that branch and in a zone with a sub-hour offset (e.g. `Asia/Kolkata` +05:30, `Asia/Kathmandu` +05:45) the run lands at :30 or :45 past the customer's local hour instead of on it.

`Schedule.Validate` (internal/exports/model.go) never checks `Timezone`, so the API accepts any string, and `NextRun` (internal/exports/schedule.go) swallows the `time.LoadLocation` error by falling back to `time.UTC`, silently reinterpreting an invalid or mistyped IANA name as UTC — a behaviour the `"unknown timezone falls back to UTC"` case in internal/exports/exports_test.go pins as correct.

`window` (internal/exports/schedule.go) returns a fixed absolute duration (24 hours daily, 7*24 hours weekly) while `NextRun` advances by calendar days at a fixed local hour in the customer's zone, so on a DST transition the local day is 23 or 25 hours and the exported window disagrees with the scheduled slot by an hour.

The cadence vocabulary is spelled out independently in four places (`Validate` in internal/exports/model.go, `NextRun` and `window` in internal/exports/schedule.go, and the `CHECK (cadence IN (...))` constraint in migrations/0057_export_schedules.sql) with no shared constant or type as `Format` has, and `window`'s `default` branch maps any unrecognised cadence to 24 hours instead of failing, so a new cadence added at some but not all sites silently exports over the wrong interval.

The only test file in the change exercises the four pure functions Validate, NextRun, objectKey and formatValue, so the newly added Store and its Create/ListByOrg/Due/Record/Delete methods, the Worker and its tick/runSchedule/export/serialize path, and the three internal/api export handlers all ship with no test that executes them.

TestValidateRejectsBadInput exercises only the SecretKey arm of Validate's credentials guard (AccessKey == "" || SecretKey == "") — the no credentials case clears SecretKey alone — so removing the AccessKey operand from model.go would leave the suite green.

Validate's guards are pinned only by rejected values, with HourOfDay tested at 24 against a single mid-range accepting fixture of 3 and no case at the adjacent accepted values 0 or 23 nor at the rejected -1, so a shifted or over-tight boundary in s.HourOfDay < 0 || s.HourOfDay > 23 survives the suite.

`Worker.runSchedule` passes the whole `s.Destination` struct as a slog attribute in the `"export failed"` log call, so the customer's `AccessKey` and `SecretKey` are written into the application log on every failed run.

`objectKey` names the object with only the dataset, the calendar date and the format, so successive runs of an hourly schedule (and two schedules sharing dataset, format and prefix) compute the same key and each upload overwrites the previous object.

The JSONL branch of `serialize` puts the raw `rows.Scan` values into the record instead of routing them through `formatValue`, so `[]byte` columns are base64-encoded and `time.Time` values are not normalised to UTC RFC 3339, making JSONL output differ from CSV output for the same row.

The `LIMIT maxRows` (500,000) cap in `Worker.export` truncates an oversized window with no way for the code to detect that the cap was reached, so a short object is uploaded, the run is recorded `succeeded`, and the schedule advances past the rows that were dropped.

The export window is a fixed `window(cadence)` duration measured back from `startedAt = time.Now().UTC()` rather than from the previous run's coverage or the scheduled slot, so scheduling jitter, restarts and DST transitions make consecutive runs leave gaps or duplicate rows.

`Worker.export` projects `SELECT *` from the mapped analytics table, so the exported column set — and the CSV header and JSONL keys derived from `rows.Columns()` — is whatever the internal table currently holds, including internal columns such as `org_id` and any column a later migration adds.

`serialize` never checks `rows.Err()` after its `for rows.Next()` loop, so an iteration cut short by a driver or connection error is indistinguishable from a completed scan and the truncated buffer is uploaded and recorded as succeeded.

`Worker.export` accumulates the entire serialized export in a single `bytes.Buffer` and hands `buf.Bytes()` to `client.Put`, so peak memory is the whole object with no streaming path and no bound other than the row cap.

Cell values are written into the CSV by `formatValue` and `csv.Writer` without neutralising a leading `=`, `+`, `-`, `@`, tab or CR, so exported event data is interpreted as a formula when the customer opens the file in a spreadsheet.

The export path derives no per-run deadline — the worker's long-lived context is passed straight to `QueryContext` and `client.Put` — and `tick` runs the due batch serially, so one hung query or upload blocks every other schedule indefinitely.

`runSchedule` calls `w.store.Record` with the same context that `Run` cancels at shutdown, so a cancellation after a successful upload also cancels the write that would have advanced `next_run_at` and recorded the outcome.

`Worker.export` interpolates `datasets[s.Dataset]` into the query without the comma-ok check that `Schedule.Validate` uses, so a stored schedule whose dataset is not in the map yields an empty table name and malformed SQL instead of a named failure.

Nothing claims a due schedule — `Due` is a plain `SELECT` with no lock or lease and `next_run_at` is advanced only by `Record` after the upload finishes — so the same due run is executed by every live worker and by repeated ticks of the same worker, contrary to the documented one-worker claim.

The raw wrapped error from `export` is stored verbatim as `last_error` via `runSchedule`'s `runErr = err.Error()` and returned to the customer by `GET /v1/export-schedules`, exposing driver text, internal table names and host details.
A failed `w.store.Record` in `runSchedule` is only logged, so `next_run_at` is never advanced and the schedule stays due and is re-exported on every subsequent 30-second poll.

`formatValue`'s `default: return fmt.Sprint(t)` renders `float64` columns in Go's default notation, so large or small values are written to the CSV in scientific notation, and the test table covers every other driver type but no float.

`ORDER BY occurred_at` in `Worker.export` is not a total order because `occurred_at` is a non-unique wall-clock timestamp, so the relative order of rows sharing an instant — and hence any cut made at that boundary — is undefined.
`Worker.Run` waits on `ticker.C` before its first `tick`, so a freshly started worker does nothing for a full poll interval even when schedules are already overdue.
`formatValue` renders a SQL NULL as the empty string, making NULL indistinguishable from a legitimately empty value in the exported CSV.
`serialize` returns `out.Error()`, the `csv.Writer`'s error, on the JSONL path where that writer is never written to, so the function's terminal error check is unconditionally nil for JSONL exports.

`s.Destination.Region` is passed straight into `storage.Config` although `Schedule.Validate` never constrains it, leaving the customer-supplied region unvalidated before it reaches the storage client.
The window filters on `occurred_at`, so a row inserted after the run whose window covered its `occurred_at` is never exported by any run.

`objectKey` dates the object with the UTC calendar date of `startedAt` while the run hour is interpreted in the customer's timezone, so the filename can name a different day than the local day whose data it contains.
`Worker` holds both a `*Store` and the raw `*sql.DB` and `export` queries `w.db` directly while every other read goes through `Store`, giving the package two data-access paths to the same database.

`dueBatchSize = 25` caps how many schedules a tick takes and they are run serially, a limit the documentation does not mention, so schedules sharing a popular slot are deferred to later ticks and can accumulate a backlog.

Deleting a schedule while a run is in flight does not signal the worker, so `(*Worker).runSchedule` still uploads that run's object to the customer's bucket and its subsequent `Store.Record` silently updates no row.

`(*exportHandler).create` and `(*exportHandler).list` dereference the result of `auth.OrgFromContext(r.Context())` immediately with no nil check, so a request that reaches the handler without an org in the context would panic.
`(*exportHandler).create` maps every `h.store.Create` failure to a 500 with a fixed message, so a client-caused constraint violation is reported to the caller as a server error instead of a 4xx.

docs/scheduled-exports.md states guarantees the rest of the change does not implement: destination credentials stored encrypted, credentials never handed back by the API, consecutive runs tiling the timeline with no gaps and no duplicated rows, no run overwriting an object an earlier run wrote, and a due schedule claimed by one worker.

docs/scheduled-exports.md contradicts itself about the same artifact: the What lands in your bucket section promises that concatenating everything a schedule produced yields the dataset with no gaps, while the Failures section says a failed run is never retried and leaves one missing file.

`Schedule.Validate` accepts and enforces `HourOfDay` for `hourly` schedules although `NextRun` ignores it for that cadence, so a value with no effect is stored and echoed back in the list response as though it were in effect.

`Schedule.LastError` carries `json:"last_error,omitempty"` while the column defaults to `''`, so the key disappears from the `GET /v1/export-schedules` payload whenever a schedule is healthy, unlike `LastStatus`, although docs/scheduled-exports.md describes both as fields the endpoint returns.

The `export_schedules` column list is written out three times — `scheduleColumns`, `Store.Create`'s INSERT, and `Store.query`'s `rows.Scan` — kept aligned only by positional order, so transposing the adjacent same-typed `dest_access_key` and `dest_secret_key` compiles and silently swaps the two credentials.
`migrations/0057_export_schedules.sql` gives `export_schedules` a `created_at` column but no `updated_at`, so nothing on the row records when a schedule was last modified.

`NextRun`'s `time.LoadLocation(s.Timezone)` requires an IANA zone database that this change never establishes for the worker's runtime image (no system tzdata and no `time/tzdata` import), so if the image ships without one every schedule silently falls back to UTC.

TestObjectKeyIsDatedAndSitsUnderThePrefix and TestFormatValueRendersScalarsForCSV exercise only inputs that already render correctly — objectKey solely for a daily UTC schedule, and formatValue with no float64, no plain string and no non-UTC time.Time — so the input shapes whose rendering is in doubt are covered by nothing.

Every case in TestValidateRejectsBadInput asserts only that Validate returned a non-nil error and never which rule fired, so a Validate rewritten to return one constant error for every input would pass the whole table.
`objectKey` uses the raw `Format` enum value as the customer-visible file extension, so changing the spelling of a `Format` constant silently changes every future object name.

`contentType` decides the MIME type in its own `if format == FormatCSV` branch while `objectKey` derives the file extension from the `Format` value, so a format added to the `Format` constants gets a correct extension but silently inherits `application/x-ndjson`.

The worker loop `Run`/`tick`/`runSchedule` has no `recover`, unlike the HTTP surface which this same change mounts behind `withRecovery` in internal/api/router.go, so a panic during one schedule's export terminates the whole worker process.

`Worker.export` calls `storage.NewClient` on every run instead of caching a client per destination, so a fresh client and its underlying transport are built and discarded for each schedule on each tick.
`objectKey` trims the slashes from `Destination.Prefix` and then always rejoins it with a `/`, so a prefix a customer intended as a filename prefix (`exports-`) is turned into a directory segment.

`runSchedule` computes `next := NextRun(s, startedAt)` and passes it to `Record` on the failure branch as well as the success branch, so a failed run advances `next_run_at` with no retry or backoff and that window's rows are covered by no later run.

`runSchedule` derives the next slot with `NextRun(s, startedAt)` from the instant the run started rather than from when it finished, so an export that overruns its cadence records a `next_run_at` that is already in the past.
Nothing in the change constructs or starts a `Worker` — neither `NewWorker` nor `Worker.Run` has a caller anywhere in the diff — so no schedule is ever executed.

`runSchedule` executes the `Schedule` value handed back by `Store.Due` without re-running `Validate` on it, so a stored row whose fields no longer satisfy the API's validation rules is exported unchecked.
